Part 1 · Seeing the invisible
01From one cell to a whole bodyLevels of organisation20 XP

Some living things are one single cell. You are made of millions.

Your breathing is built in layers. Tap them in order, smallest first.
0 of 5 placed

Similar cells doing similar work make a tissue. Tissues make an organ. Organs working together make an organ system — nasal pores, nasal cavity, trachea and lungs make the respiratory system. Even so, the cell stays the fundamental unit. Nothing smaller is alive.

A creature made of one cell is unicellular; one made of many is multicellular. Bacteria and yeast are unicellular. Plants, fish, birds and humans are not.

Curiosity · Life probably began in water. In the hot springs of Puga Valley in Ladakh, water sits near boiling point even in a cold climate — close to conditions on Earth 3.5 billion years ago. The heat-loving bacteria there, called thermophiles, are unicellular.
02Where the eye gives upLimit of resolution · the scale of life30 XP

Imagine two dots on paper moving closer together. At about 25 cm from your eye, two points stay separate only while they are at least 0.1 mm apart. Closer than that and they merge into one. This is the limit of resolution of the human eye — and almost every cell is below it.

Drag below 1 mm and the view has to switch instrument. That handover is the whole reason cell biology waited for the microscope.
Which of these could you NOT see as a separate object with the unaided eye?
0.1 mm is 100 µm, so a 60 µm cell falls below the limit. A 1 mm fish egg is ten times larger than the limit and is easily visible.
03Label the microscopeParts, magnification, Robert Hooke30 XP

Robert Hooke was the first person to see a cell, in 1665, with a microscope he designed himself at about 200–300× magnification. Looking at a thin slice of cork he saw small box-like compartments and named them cells.

Tap a marked part, then tap its name.
0 of 8 labelled
Total magnification = eyepiece × objective.
Electron microscopes go much further. They use a beam of electrons instead of light and resolve structure down to the nanometre — one-billionth of a metre.
04Estimate the size of a cellActivity 2.125 XP

You cannot put a ruler against one cell. So you measure the whole circular field of view in millimetres, convert to micrometres, then count how many cells lie across it in a straight line and divide.

1 mm = 1000 µm

A field is 4 mm wide and you count 20 cells across it. How big is one cell?
4 mm is 4000 µm. Divided among 20 cells, each is 200 µm across — the size the chapter gives for an onion peel cell.
Part 2 · The boundary of a cell
05GatekeeperCell membrane · fluid-mosaic model35 XP

The cell membrane is a thin boundary, only 7 to 10 nanometres thick, that surrounds every cell and defines its individuality. It is made of lipids and proteins. Two layers of fat molecules sit with their water-attracting heads facing outwards and water-repelling tails facing inwards — the lipid bilayer — with proteins embedded among them.

Those molecules slide sideways, flip and rotate, so the membrane is fluid. The molecules sit together like tiles in a mosaic. Hence the fluid-mosaic model. The embedded proteins act as gatekeepers.

The membrane is selectively permeable. Decide what gets through.

06The osmosis benchDiffusion, osmosis, tonicity40 XP

Put one potato piece in plain water and another in salty water. An hour later the first has gained weight and the second has lost it. Nothing was added or removed. Where did the weight go?

Solution
—
Rhoeo peel · has a wall
—
Cheek cell · no wall
—

Water moves from where there is more of it to where there is less, until both sides even out. That movement of water through a membrane has a name: osmosis. It is how water from soil enters root cells.

The wider idea is diffusion — particles spreading from where they are crowded to where they are not. That happens even with no membrane in the way. Osmosis is just diffusion of water, across a membrane that lets water through and holds the salt back.

Cell X in pure water swells; Cell Y in concentrated salt shrinks. Why?
The membrane is selectively permeable — water passes, salt does not. Nothing enters Cell Y at all. Osmosis moves water alone, from the dilute side toward the concentrated side.
07The wall that holdsCell wall · plasmolysis25 XP

Plants cannot walk away from wind and rain, so they need rigidity. Outside the cell membrane, plant cells carry an extra covering of cellulose — the cell wall. Fungi and bacteria have one too. It keeps leaves and flowers firm and holds the plant upright.

The wall is rigid but permeable — water and dissolved minerals pass straight through. Only the membrane inside it is selective. Cellulose in your diet passes through undigested as roughage.

Mark each statement true or false.
0 of 5
In 20 per cent sugar solution the outer boundary of a Rhoeo cell stays exactly where it was, while the contents shrink away from it and the gap between them widens. A cheek cell, with no wall, simply collapses.
Part 3 · Inside the cell
08Fill in Table 2.1Prokaryotic vs eukaryotic35 XP

Here are three cells. Look at what each one has — and what it is missing.

Now fill the table from the pictures. Tap a box to cycle blank → present → absent.

You have just found the deepest split in biology. The bacterial cell has no proper nucleus — its genetic material sits loose in a region called the nucleoid — and none of its parts are wrapped in their own membranes. Cells like that are prokaryotic (pro = primitive, karyon = nucleus).

Plant and animal cells have a proper nucleus and many wrapped compartments called organelles, sitting in the jelly-like cytoplasm. Those are eukaryotic cells (eu = true).

A prokaryotic cell is 1 to 10 µm across and usually unicellular. A eukaryotic cell is 10 to 100 µm and may be unicellular or multicellular.
09The cell factoryMatch each organelle to its job45 XP

A cell is a tiny living factory and every part has a specific job. Organelles build new materials, remove waste and supply energy, all at the same time and independently of each other.

Tap an organelle, then tap the job it does.
0 of 9 matched
Mitochondria and plastids both carry their own DNA and their own ribosomes, so they can make some of their own proteins — a strong hint that both share an evolutionary history with single-celled organisms.
10From nucleus to DNAFour steps down35 XP

The nucleus has a double-layered nuclear membrane with pores that let material move between the nucleus and the cytoplasm. Inside sits the nucleolus, the dense round body where ribosomal subunits are made before leaving for the cytoplasm.

Mature red blood cells have no nucleus at all. That empty space carries more haemoglobin and more oxygen — but with no nucleus they cannot repair or divide, and survive only about 120 days.
11The protein journeyRibosome → ER → Golgi → membrane35 XP

Rough ER looks rough because ribosomes are stuck to its surface; it handles protein synthesis and secretion, as in the gland cells of the pancreas. Smooth ER has no ribosomes and deals in fats and hormones. The Golgi apparatus is the cell's post office — it modifies, sorts and packages material into vesicles.

Lysosomes are single membrane-bound sacs of enzymes that break down unwanted proteins, carbohydrates, fats and worn-out organelles, keeping the cell clean. They are formed by the Golgi apparatus too.
12Why plants wiltVacuole, cell sap and turgor30 XP

A mature plant cell usually holds one large central vacuole, surrounded by a selectively permeable membrane and filled with a watery fluid called cell sap. It stores water, minerals, sugars and waste. By holding all that water it keeps pressure up inside the cell, and that pressure keeps the plant firm.

Animal cells have vacuoles too, but small ones, used only for temporary storage.
Part 4 · How cells continue
13Mitosis and meiosisCount the chromosomes45 XP

A cut heals. Fallen hair grows back. Both happen because cells divide. Set a chromosome count and run each kind of division — watch what comes out.

Mitosis makes two daughter cells identical to the parent, with the same DNA and the same chromosome number. This is growth, repair and healing. When you get taller it is not that your cells got bigger — a cell can only grow so far — it is that they divided. About one per cent of your cells are replaced every day.

Meiosis divides twice instead of once and makes four gametes, each with half the chromosomes. It happens only in reproductive organs — testes and ovaries in animals, anthers and ovaries in plants. Halving now is what lets fertilisation restore the full number later.

If gametes were formed by mitosis instead of meiosis, what would happen at fertilisation?
Meiosis halves the chromosome number so that fusion of two gametes restores the original count. Skip the halving and each generation would inherit twice as many chromosomes as the last.
14When cells stop stoppingContact inhibition and tumours35 XP

Cells grow and divide in a controlled way, stay where they belong, do their work, and die when they are no longer needed. In many animal cells, division stops as soon as a cell touches its neighbours. That brake is called contact inhibition. Cancer cells lose it and keep dividing, forming tumours.

Plant cells do not show contact inhibition at all — their rigid walls mean they grow to a different pattern entirely. Cells also have a built-in way of dying on purpose: programmed cell death. It is what removes the tissue between an embryo's fingers. Without it, we would have webbed hands.
15Building the cell theoryPut the discoveries in order30 XP

The classical cell theory says three things: all living organisms are made of one or more cells; the cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living beings; and all cells arise from pre-existing cells. It unites all of biology, from bacteria to humans.

Tap the discoveries in order, earliest first.

Camillo Golgi's apparatus was doubted for decades because early microscopes could not resolve it — electron microscopy confirmed it long after his death. Arun Kumar Sharma, a Padma Bhushan botanist, invented many of the lab methods used to study chromosomes in plants.
